question: Simpson's paradox: how can a treatment win every test but lose overall?

research.claim: In a 1986 kidney-stone study, treatment A (open surgery) succeeded more often than treatment B (a closed procedure) for small stones (81 of 87, 93%, against 234 of 270, 87%) and for large stones (192 of 263, 73%, against 55 of 80, 69%), yet B succeeded more often overall (289 of 350, 83%, against 273 of 350, 78%). This reversal, Simpson's paradox, happens because A was given mostly large stones, which are harder to treat, so its overall rate is weighted toward its lower large-stone rate.
research.explanation: Each treatment's overall success rate is an average of its small-stone and large-stone rates, weighted by how many of its patients had each kind of stone. Large stones fail more often under either treatment. A treated 263 large stones and only 87 small ones, so its overall rate (78%) sits close to its large-stone rate (73%); B treated 270 small stones and only 80 large ones, so its overall rate (83%) sits close to its small-stone rate (87%). Comparing the totals therefore compares mostly hard cases for A with mostly easy cases for B. With the same mix of stones, A would win overall too. Stone size is the lurking, or confounding, variable: doctors tended to give the harder, large-stone cases the better treatment A. The same pattern appeared in Berkeley's graduate admissions for fall 1973: 44% of the men who applied were admitted against 35% of the women, but department by department the data showed a small but statistically significant bias in favour of women, because women tended to apply to more competitive departments. Edward H. Simpson described the phenomenon in 1951; Karl Pearson (1899) and Udny Yule (1903) had mentioned similar effects, and Colin R. Blyth named it Simpson's paradox in 1972.
assumptions: The counts are those reported for the study; each tile in the picture is one patient.
Stone size is the only difference between the groups considered.
research.prediction: Weighting each treatment's group success rates by its own mix of stone sizes reproduces its overall rate, and with equal mixes A's overall rate is higher.
research.falsifier: If A's overall rate could not be written as its small and large rates weighted by its patient mix, the explanation would be wrong.
limitations: Which treatment is better depends on how patients were assigned; the study was not randomized, so other differences may matter too.
Real decisions also weigh risks and costs, not only success rates.
misconceptions: Overall numbers always tell the truth: a hidden difference in the groups can reverse them.
A treatment that wins in every group must win overall: not when the groups are mixed in different proportions.

scene.title: Simpson's paradox: how can a treatment win every test but lose overall?
scene.subtitle: Treatment A beat treatment B for small kidney stones and for large ones. Yet overall, B came out ahead. How?
scene.why: Totals can point the wrong way. In a real kidney-stone study, one treatment did better for small stones and for large ones, and still looked worse overall.
scene.opening: Can a treatment be better for every patient and still worse overall?

beats.title: Overall
beats.body: Imagine two treatments for kidney stones, each tried on 350 patients. Treatment A worked for 78% of its patients, and treatment B for 83%. So B looks like the better treatment.

beats.title: Small stones
beats.body: Now split the patients by the size of their stone. For small stones, A worked 93% of the time, and B only 87%. On small stones, A is the better treatment.

beats.title: Large stones
beats.body: For large stones, A wins again: 73% against 69%. So A is better for small stones and for large ones. Yet B still wins overall, so how can both be true?

beats.title: Who got what
beats.body: Look at which patients got which treatment. Of A's 350 patients, 263 had large stones; of B's, only 80. Large stones are harder: both treatments work less often on them.

beats.title: Simpson's paradox
beats.body: A's total is mostly hard cases, so it leans toward 73%; B's toward 87%. When adding groups together flips the winner, it's called Simpson's paradox. Before comparing totals, ask what else differs between the groups.

scene.takeaway: A treatment can win in every group and still lose overall when the groups are mixed in different proportions, so compare like with like.

questions.a: A, as far as this study shows: it did better on small stones and on large ones. B only looked better overall because it was given mostly the easier, small-stone cases. The patients were not assigned at random, so other differences could still matter.
Yes. A 1986 study compared treatments for kidney stones; treatment A was open surgery and treatment B a closed procedure.

questions.q: Why did A get the harder cases?
questions.a: Doctors tended to give the harder, large-stone cases to A, the treatment that did better, and the easier small stones to B.

In 1973 Berkeley admitted 44% of the men who applied and 35% of the women. Department by department the gap vanished, with a small bias in favour of women: women had mostly applied to departments that were harder to get into.

questions.q: Why is it called Simpson's paradox?
questions.a: Edward Simpson described it in a 1951 paper; Karl Pearson and Udny Yule had noticed similar effects earlier, and Colin Blyth gave it the name in 1972.

physics_review.summary: Every number and historical fact matches the retrieved page: the kidney-stone counts and rates (81/87, 234/270, 192/263, 55/80; 273/350 and 289/350), A as open and B as closed surgery, the 1986 study, stone size as the lurking variable with large stones given to A, Berkeley 1973 (44% and 35%, with a small bias in favour of women by department), Simpson 1951, Pearson 1899, Yule 1903 and Blyth 1972. Tile counts in the frames match the data exactly. Round 2 fixed the overclaims: 'as far as this study shows', the not-at-random caveat, and the why line.
changes: The new FAQ on why A got the harder cases should not guess at the doctors' reasons (applied).

visual_review.summary: All round-1 problems are fixed: in chapter 4 the shading and the 263 and 80 counts are on screen when the subtitle quotes them; the overall pills sit level on rules below both columns; the chapter 5 outlines make each combined total a visible whole. The reversal reads at a glance: A's column is mostly a large shaded block and B's mostly small stones. Labels are few and short and the phone layout works.
changes: Optional: centre the picture vertically on desktop; larger pills on a phone.

learner_review.summary: Explanation: A beats B within each stone size, but 263 of A's 350 patients had the hard large stones and only 80 of B's did, so A's overall rate leans toward its 73% and B's toward its 87%; comparing the totals mostly compares a hard caseload with an easy one. Round 2 supplies the missing why: chapter 4 shows large stones are harder with the evidence, chapter 5 gives the mechanism, and the FAQ explains why A got the hard cases. Every line is at most 80 characters, three per chapter, and reads naturally aloud.

blind_review.summary: Blind reading matched all five chapters: two 350-square grids, A 78% and B 83%; each splits into small and large groups, A winning both (93 against 87, 73 against 69) yet losing overall; the large groups highlighted with 263 and 80 patients; and outlines gathering each treatment's groups into its total. The point: unequal group sizes can make an overall rate reverse the comparison inside every group. Square counts match the numbers.
changes: Coloured squares meaning 'worked' is inferred, not labelled.
